---
title: "Figure 15.2: China's Share of Latin American Passenger Car Imports"
---

![Python: `python/fig-15-2.py`](../images/python/fig-15-2.png)

China's share of passenger car imports in Latin America: the regional
average as a line, and the range across countries as a shaded area. The
bottom of the band is the country with the lowest share in that year, the
top the country with the highest. The chart shows both how fast the average
has risen and how unequal the rise has been.

**A short band chart.** Together with [Figure 1.2.2](fig-1-2-2.qmd), it is
the template for a line with a min–max range. If you need to draw that kind
of chart, start from this script.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 11 rows (2015 to 2025):

| category | Min | Difference | LATAM |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2015 | 0.09 | 10.84 | 2.51 |

There is no `Max` column. In Excel, a shaded range is usually built as a
stacked area chart with two series: an invisible bottom series (`Min`) and,
stacked on top of it, a visible series that is the width of the band
(`Difference`, the maximum minus the minimum). The data extracted from the
chart therefore has these two helper series, and the script adds them up to
get the top of the band. See [Shaded bands](../techniques.qmd#sec-bands).

`LATAM` is the regional average, drawn as the line.

## The script

### The frame

```python
data = read_chart_data(STEM)
years = data["category"]

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="China's Share of Latin American Passenger Car\nImports",
    subtitle="(Percent share)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: UN Comtrade; World Bank, World Integrated Trade Solution;\n"
        "and IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Shaded area refers to the min-max range."
    ),
    left=0.3,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.3,
)
```

The years are stored once in `years`, because they are used by both the band
and the line. The title is long, so it breaks before "Imports", as in the
published chart. `new_chart()` sees the `\n` and moves the plot down by one
title line.

The caption explains the shaded area. That is why the chart needs no legend.

### The band and the line

```python
# In Excel the min-max range is a stacked area: "Min" plus "Difference".
ax.fill_between(years, data["Min"], data["Min"] + data["Difference"],
                color="#F2EDF4", linewidth=0)
ax.plot(years, data["LATAM"], color="#5B2677", linewidth=1.9,
        solid_capstyle="round")
```

`ax.fill_between(x, lower, upper)` fills the area between two curves. Here
`lower` is the minimum and `upper` is the minimum plus the difference, which
is the maximum. pandas adds the two columns row by row, so
`data["Min"] + data["Difference"]` is a new column of 11 values.

- `color="#F2EDF4"` is a very light purple, the same hue as the line but
  much paler, so the band stays in the background.
- `linewidth=0` removes the outline that matplotlib otherwise draws around a
  filled area. Excel draws the stacked area without an outline, too.

The average line comes second, so it is drawn on top of the band. In
matplotlib, as in Excel's series order, what is drawn later lies on top.
`#5B2677` is a dark purple. `solid_capstyle="round"` gives it rounded ends.

The order matters more than it seems: if you swap the two calls, the line
disappears under the band wherever the band covers it.

### The axes

```python
ax.set_xlim(2014.5, 2025.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(2015, 2026, 2))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=2.8, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, 0, 50, 10)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)
```

- **The x-axis** runs half a year beyond the first and last points, so the
  band does not touch the edges. `range(2015, 2026, 2)` labels every second
  year: 2015, 2017, ..., 2025.
- **The y-axis** runs from 0 to 50 with a tick every 10, set with the shared
  helper [`set_y_scale()`](../chart-style.qmd#sec-y-scale).
- **The tick marks** are 2.8 points long on both axes, and `pad=5` leaves a
  small gap between the x-ticks and the year labels.

The script ends with `save_chart(fig, STEM)`.

## Changing the chart

- **A different band colour.** Keep the band much lighter than the line.
  An easy way is to use the line colour with transparency:
  `color="#5B2677", alpha=0.1`.
- **A data set with `Max` instead of `Difference`.** Use
  `ax.fill_between(years, data["Min"], data["Max"], ...)` directly.
- **A legend for the band.** Add `label="Min-max range"` to `fill_between`
  and `label="Average"` to `plot`, then call `ax.legend()`. matplotlib draws
  a filled square for the band and a line for the average.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-15-2.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-15-2.py"}
"""Figure 15.2: China's Share of Latin American Passenger Car Imports."""
from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart, set_y_scale

STEM = "fig-15-2"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)
years = data["category"]

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="China's Share of Latin American Passenger Car\nImports",
    subtitle="(Percent share)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: UN Comtrade; World Bank, World Integrated Trade Solution;\n"
        "and IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Shaded area refers to the min-max range."
    ),
    left=0.3,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.3,
)

# In Excel the min-max range is a stacked area: "Min" plus "Difference".
ax.fill_between(years, data["Min"], data["Min"] + data["Difference"],
                color="#F2EDF4", linewidth=0)
ax.plot(years, data["LATAM"], color="#5B2677", linewidth=1.9,
        solid_capstyle="round")

ax.set_xlim(2014.5, 2025.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(2015, 2026, 2))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=2.8, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, 0, 50, 10)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
